We will show that if you start with the numbers 
  1, 2, 3, …, 1024
and then perform the following operation exactly ten times, namely “replace the 2k numbers on the board by the 2k–1 numbers that are the nonnegative differences of the numbers in 2k‐element pairs” (so that in the end only one number remains), then no matter how you “pair‐off” the numbers at each step the final number must be one of

Explicitly lists the set of possible final values.

sentence: Moreover, every one of these numbers can indeed be obtained by a suitable choice of pairings and choices of “order” in taking the difference.
sentence-category-reason: States that each listed value is attainable, completing the characterization of answers.

sentence: It turns out that one may “encode” any possible run of the process by the following observation.
sentence-category-reason: Introduces an analytical framework to encode runs of the process.

sentence: In each step one takes two numbers (say a and b) and erases them, writing instead the number |a – b|.
sentence-category-reason: Restates the operation performed at each step from the problem.

sentence: (Since |a–b| = |b–a| the order in which the two numbers are subtracted does not affect the number that is written, even though as we shall see a certain sign‐choice may be regarded as “hidden” in the process.
sentence-category-reason: Explains a property of the operation and hints at hidden sign choices.

sentence: ) In fact one may “keep track” of the whole process by “expressing” every number on the board as a linear combination of the original numbers 1, 2, 3, …, 1024 with coefficients +1 or –1.
sentence-category-reason: Proposes representing numbers as signed sums of the originals to track the process.

sentence-category-reason: Gives the general signed-sum form of numbers on the board.

sentence: When two numbers X and Y are “paired off” and replaced by |X–Y| one may “choose” to regard X and Y as having disappeared and then writing X–Y (or Y–X) on the board.
sentence-category-reason: Conceptually interprets replacing a pair by a difference in terms of sign choices.

sentence: In other words, at every stage one is “making a sign‐choice” in writing the new number as a signed sum of some of the original numbers.
sentence-category-reason: Summarizes the idea that each step corresponds to a sign choice in a signed sum.

sentence: (Note that although it is possible to get different algebraic expressions – even with different numbers of plus and minus signs – the number eventually written on the board is always its nonnegative value.
sentence-category-reason: Notes that different algebraic expressions map to the same nonnegative value; conceptual observation.

sentence: A short reflection on the binary‐tree “structure” of the pairing process shows that if you “list” all the sign–assignments that might arise, then the final number is always of the form
sentence-category-reason: Deduces from the pairing structure that outcomes have a specific absolute signed-sum form.

sentence: This, however, is true for many “sign–choosings” that are not obtainable by our pairing process.
sentence-category-reason: Observes that not all sign assignments correspond to valid processes; a constraint.

sentence: In fact one may show that in any process the signs that occur are not “arbitrary” but must satisfy a certain parity condition.
sentence-category-reason: States there is a parity constraint on attainable sign patterns.

sentence: (A short exercise with the cases 1,2 and 1,2,3,4 shows that while with two numbers the only possibility is 1 = |1 – 2|, with four numbers the only outcomes possible are 0 and 2.
sentence-category-reason: Checks small cases to support constraints on outcomes.

sentence: One may then “guess” that with 2ᵏ numbers the final number can never exceed 2ᵏ/2 and, moreover, when 2ᵏ numbers with k ≥ 2 are on the board the final number is always an even number.
sentence-category-reason: Posits a conjecture about bounds and parity of outcomes, using tentative language.

sentence: In our problem 1024 = 2¹⁰ so that after ten rounds the final number is even and (one may prove by induction) cannot be larger than 1024/2 = 512.
sentence-category-reason: Draws a general conclusion about parity and an upper bound from 1024 = 2^10 without performing detailed calculations.

sentence: A somewhat more detailed analysis shows that in fact every even number between 0 and 512 can be obtained.
sentence-category-reason: Claims the full range of achievable even values, asserting a property of the outcomes.

sentence:
For example, when only two numbers (namely 1 and 2) are on the board (that is, when k = 1) the only possible final number is 
  |1–2| = 1.
sentence-category-reason: Carries out a concrete computation for k=1: computes |1−2| = 1.

sentence: But when you have four numbers (that is, 1,2,3,4) one may show that no matter what choices are made the answer will always be even and in fact the only possibilities are 0 and 2.
sentence-category-reason: States derived possibilities (0 and 2) and evenness for four numbers without showing steps.

sentence: (One possible run is to pair 1 with 2 and 3 with 4 so that one obtains 1 and 1; then pairing these two gives 0.
sentence-category-reason: Executes a specific pairing sequence and computes resulting numbers leading to 0.

sentence: Another possibility is to pair 1 with 4 (which gives 3) and 2 with 3 (which gives 1); then 3 and 1 give 2.
sentence-category-reason: Executes another specific pairing sequence and computes resulting numbers leading to 2.

sentence: ) Similar examples may be found in the case of 8 numbers; one may obtain 0, 2, or 4.
sentence-category-reason: States the possible outcomes for eight numbers without detailed computation.

sentence: (In that case one may show that the final number cannot exceed 8/2 = 4.
sentence-category-reason: Infers an upper bound (≤ 4) for eight numbers; a deductive statement.

sentence:
Thus one may prove by induction that if we start with 2ᵏ numbers then
  – if k = 1 the only final number is 1, and
  – if k ≥ 2 the final number is an even number that never exceeds 2ᵏ/2.
sentence-category-reason: Summarizes an inductive result describing all cases for 2^k numbers.

sentence:
In our problem k = 10 so that the only possible final numbers are
  0, 2, 4, …, 512.
sentence-category-reason: Applies the general result to k=10 and explicitly lists all possible final numbers.

sentence:
A more “combinatorial‐invariance” approach can be made rigorous by showing that if one writes
  final = (1+2+⋯+1024) – 2K,
where K is the sum of certain “minima” taken in the various steps, then K can take on all appropriate values so that final runs through all even numbers from 0 to 512.
sentence-category-reason: Describes an invariant-based formula and deduces the range of final values.
